items.title: Scaling Git for the agentic software factory
items.summary: AI agents are fundamentally changing the economics of software development. As the cost of producing code falls, the volume of changes moving through the software factory is accelerating beyond what infrastructure designed for human developers was built to handle.GitLab anticipated this shift and began developing next-generation source code management (SCM) to support thousands of concurrent agents working against large repositories. In June, we announced next-gen SCM at GitLab Transcend, joined on stage by Nick G. from Anthropic's source control team. We've continued collaborating on the technical challenges of agent-scale development, and in August we shared more of our architecture and early performance results.This week, Anthropic provided a compelling demonstration of why this work is so important. As daily merges to its monorepo grew from approximately 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September, its engineers built Scion, a specialized source control system designed for their environment.Anthropic's experience reinforces the architectural direction we've been pursuing. Scion is purpose-built for enormous monorepos where nearly all clients are agents that are always online. Anthropic acknowledges that its approach isn't a general-purpose replacement for Git and requires its own code review, search, and CI infrastructure.GitLab is building for the broader enterprise market: delivering agent-scale performance while preserving Git compatibility, infrastructure choice, and integration with the software development lifecycle."Scaling our monorepo for agentic development has changed how we think about Git server architecture. We see room to expand what Git servers can do for these workloads without departing from the overall Git model."— Nick G., Source Control, AnthropicBuilt on Git. Designed for agents.Traditional Git workflows require clients to download substantial repository data, even when an agent needs only a small portion. A single agent invocation can involve 5–10 GB of data transfer and more than 30 seconds of setup, just to answer one question. Multiply that overhead across thousands of agents and source control becomes a bottleneck.Most enterprises can't move source control onto new infrastructure just to scale it. Next-gen SCM preserves the Git protocol while modernizing the architecture underneath. Stateless compute scales horizontally against shared object storage, while agent-native interfaces let agents request the files and history they need without repeatedly cloning entire repositories.In early internal tests, workloads completed up to 50x faster, used up to 2x fewer tokens, and generated up to 1,000x less network traffic compared with conventional workflows. These are peak improvements under specific test conditions, and we're continuing to validate performance under sustained, concurrent load.The same architecture is designed to run on GitLab.com and on S3-compatible storage that customers control, including in air-gapped data centers. Repository data stays within the customer's infrastructure, preserving data sovereignty and existing investments while delivering the scalability agentic development demands.For a closer look at the architecture and what we're building, watch Mark and Kranthi's latest next-gen SCM update:Source control is only the first bottleneckSpeeding up source control alone moves the bottleneck downstream. An agent that writes code in seconds creates little value if the resulting changes spend hours waiting for validation, security review, or deployment.Traditional merge queues and CI workflows face growing pressure when agents generate changes faster than validation can complete. We're seeing this pressure across GitLab.com. Over the past year, customers created 40% more CI/CD pipelines, while code pushes increased 50%. Agent-scale CI will need to validate more changes with less compute per change while preserving evidence of what was tested and verified.This is why next-gen SCM is part of GitLab's broader vision for a governed software factory. As agents accelerate software production, source control, context, orchestration, CI, security, and governance must evolve together.We're designing next-gen SCM to let thousands of agents work in parallel in isolated sessions, where unsuccessful experiments can be discarded without disrupting shared code. Successful changes can flow into GitLab's existing merge requests, pipelines, security checks, and governance controls on their path to production.GitLab Orbit is being developed to provide a context graph of the entire software lifecycle, while GitLab Duo Agent Platform orchestrates agent work across stages.
